issues: Wrong history in the correction. It says 'For decades the Bureau acknowledged releasing block-level data'. The opposite is true. The acknowledgement dates only from 2000: Anderson and Seltzer documented the tract and block data that year, and director Kenneth Prewitt apologised in 2000. SciAm opens with 'Despite decades of denials', and Seltzer and Anderson (Social Research 2001, p. 492) say the bureau 'has denied the charge' that microdata were released.

Overreach by omission. The correction does not say that the 2007 records cover only the Washington, D.C., area. SciAm: 'The records, however, do not indicate that the Bureau was asked for or divulged such information for Japanese-Americans in other parts of the country.' Added, so readers do not infer that name lists were used for the West Coast removal.
Typo: 'an 4 August 1943' should be 'a 4 August 1943'. The request came from Treasury Secretary Henry Morgenthau, which is now named.

Checked OK: the SciAm quote is verbatim (FOUND); the title, the 30 March 2007 date and the author JR Minkel match; the data were released seven days after the request; the documents were found in the records of the Commerce Department's chief clerk; Prewitt was Census director 1998-2000 and said 'The [new] evidence is convincing'. The FALSE verdict on the claim 'never names' stands.

fieldFixes.correction: For decades the Census Bureau denied giving other agencies individual “microdata”. By 2000 it had acknowledged, and director Kenneth Prewitt had apologised for, releasing neighbourhood-level (tract and block) data used in the removal of Japanese Americans. In 2007 Margo Anderson and William Seltzer found Commerce Department records showing that the Bureau gave the Treasury, for the Secret Service, the names and locations of people of Japanese ancestry in the Washington, D.C., area. It did so seven days after a 4 August 1943 request from Treasury Secretary Henry Morgenthau. The records show no such lists for other parts of the country. Prewitt, Census director from 1998 to 2000, called the new evidence convincing.

sourceFixes.note: Re-fetched: quote FOUND. Also FOUND on the page: 'Despite decades of denials, government records confirm that the U.S. Census Bureau provided the U.S. Secret Service with names and addresses of Japanese-Americans during World War II'; the Morgenthau request of 4 August 1943 for the Washington, D.C., area; 'The records, however, do not indicate that the Bureau was asked for or divulged such information for Japanese-Americans in other parts of the country'; release 'just seven days after it was requested'; Prewitt 'issued a public apology in 2000 for the Bureau's release of neighborhood data'. The title, date (30 March 2007) and byline (JR Minkel) match.

issues: The last sentence overstates the case and conflicts with a source used elsewhere in this slice. It lists '1939 supplementary cards' and 'census returns' among 'the decisive tools'. The Bundesarchiv essay on those cards (Zimmermann) says their use for the deportations 'could not be proved so far ... and is rather unlikely', because the cards reached the registration offices only in April/May 1941 and the Reich Office of Genealogy in January 1942. USHMM, the source cited here, names 'paper records and local knowledge': Jewish community records, parish records, tax records, police records and registries, compulsory self-identification, and denunciation. It does not name census returns. Rewritten to follow USHMM. The Dutch example is kept: Seltzer and Anderson (p. 487) say the Dutch registers and identity cards 'played an important role'.
Minor precision: the machines were introduced at the concentration-camp headquarters in 1942 and tracked living prisoners, 'particularly' their occupational skills. The date is now given.

Checked OK: the USHMM quote is verbatim (FOUND) and the title 'Locating the Victims' is right; the 1939 census recorded 'race'; Hollerith was an IBM subsidiary; 'About 75%, or 4.5 million of the 6 million Jews killed ... lived in Poland, the Baltics ... and the Soviet Union'. Edwin Black's IBM and the Holocaust is from 2001. The MISLEADING verdict is appropriate.

fieldFixes.correction: Hollerith punch-card machines, made by IBM's German subsidiary, did tabulate German census data, including the 1939 census's “race” data. From 1942 they were used at the headquarters of the concentration-camp system to track living prisoners, especially their occupational skills. But the US Holocaust Memorial Museum stresses that locating and identifying victims “did not rely on modern technology”. That was done with paper records (Jewish community lists, church, tax and police records, compulsory self-registration) and with local knowledge and denunciation. About 4.5 million of the 6 million Jews killed lived in Poland, the Baltics and the Soviet Union, where such machines would not have been found. In the occupied Netherlands, the population register and its identity cards played an important role in rounding Jews up. Edwin Black's IBM and the Holocaust (2001) argues for a larger role for the machines.

sourceFixes.note: Re-fetched: quote FOUND. Also on the page (read in full): 'The Germans and their collaborators used paper records and local knowledge to identify Jews to be rounded up or killed. Records included those created by Jewish communities of their members, parish records of Protestant and Catholic churches (for converted Jews), government tax records, and police records, including registries of Jews compiled by local, collaborating police.' The 1942 camp-headquarters sentence and the 75% / 4.5 million sentence quoted in the existing note are verbatim.

issues: Wrong year for the metric. 25,000 is the number of prints the complaint alleges had been circulated 'before the commencement of the action'. The action was already being decided on demurrer at Monroe County Special Term in August 1900 (32 Misc. 344), so the prints were in circulation by 1900. The Appellate Division ruled in July 1901 (64 A.D. 30). 1902 is only the year of the Court of Appeals opinion that repeats the figure. Year changed to 1900. The record id can stay.

Geography too narrow. The complaint alleged the lithographs were posted 'throughout the United States and other countries, and particularly in the vicinity where the plaintiff resides' (Special Term, 1900; the Appellate Division and Gray's dissent say the same). 'New York State (Rochester area)' understates the allegation.

Framing: the figure and 'without consent' are allegations in the complaint, which the Court of Appeals took as true on demurrer. They are not findings of fact. The notes say so, but the label states it as fact, so the label is now qualified.
Checked OK: the quote is verbatim on the Hofstra copy (FOUND); the opinion date of 27 June 1902, the citation 171 N.Y. 538 and 'about 25,000' match the Caselaw Access Project text of 171 N.Y. 538.

issues: The label is slightly overstated. 'People counted with Hollerith punch-card tabulators' implies that the headcount itself was made from punch cards. The Census Bureau source says 'tabulated data for nearly 63 million people using Hollerith's tabulators'. Wikipedia's article on the 1890 census says the rough family count of 62,947,714 was produced in six weeks on Hollerith tabulators with the card reader replaced by a keyboard: 'punched cards were not used for this tabulation'. Punched cards were used for the detailed population tabulations. The label now follows the source wording.

Checked OK: the quote is verbatim (FOUND); the page title 'History and the Census: Herman Hollerith and Mechanical Tabulation' (by Jason G. Gauthier) and the January 2016 date match the URL. The value of 63,000,000 ('nearly 63 million') agrees with the independently reported 1890 totals of 62,947,714 (rough count) and 62,979,766 (final resident population).

issues: The population is ambiguous. 277,500 (Table 1: 277,531) is the essay's 'Total number of people of Jewish origin' under the Nazi classification. It is made up of 203,765 'Jews' (at least three Jewish grandparents), 45,982 'Jewish half-breeds of first degree' (two Jewish grandparents) and 27,784 'of second degree' (one Jewish grandparent). A reader of the label 'People of Jewish origin' could take all 277,500 as Jews. The label now names the Nazi classification, and the notes give the breakdown.

Wrong territory. 'German Reich' should be the pre-1938 Reich (the 'Altreich'). The essay's official comparison figures are the census results for the Reich in its borders of 1 January 1938, without Austria and the Sudetenland: 52,005 first-degree and 32,669 second-degree 'Mischlinge', which exactly match the Altreich column of de.wikipedia's Volkszählung 1939 table. Austria alone counted a further 94,530 'Volljuden'. So the 87.2% coverage figure refers to the Altreich only.

Missing areas incomplete. Besides Thuringia and the Rhine Province, the cards for the administrative districts of Erfurt and Minden and for some Bavarian districts were not passed on. 'some other areas' is acceptable but vague, so the notes are now more precise.

Checked OK: the quote is verbatim (FOUND); author Nicolai M. Zimmermann; title matches the PDF header; about 130,000 households; 87.2% (Table 1 gives 87.21%). Note that the cards covered every person in the household, so they also list 126,599 non-Jewish persons (Table 1 total 410,920). The 277,500 figure correctly excludes them.

fieldFixes.notes: Table 1 gives 277,531, in about 130,000 households: 203,765 classed as 'Jews' (three or more Jewish grandparents), 45,982 as first-degree and 27,784 as second-degree 'Mischlinge'. Cards for Thuringia, the Rhine Province, the districts of Erfurt and Minden and some Bavarian districts were never passed on.
